options.text: How many assertions each test makes

questions.explanation: Coverage reports the fraction of code that ran during tests — execution, not correctness or assertion quality.

questions.prompt: Why is branch coverage stronger than line coverage?

options.text: It requires each decision to go both true and false, catching untested else/false paths

questions.explanation: A single input can execute every line while only taking one side of an if; branch coverage flags the untaken branch.

questions.prompt: Why can 100% coverage still miss bugs? Select all that apply.

options.text: A test can run a line while asserting nothing meaningful
Coverage doesn't ensure you tried the inputs where bugs live
Covered code can be fully executed and still be wrong
Coverage proves the absence of all defects

questions.explanation: Coverage measures execution, not assertions, inputs, or correctness — it can never prove the absence of defects.

questions.prompt: 'When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure' is known as ____'s law.
questions.explanation: Goodhart's law explains why mandating a coverage target invites tests that game the number.

questions.prompt: Order coverage types from weakest to most rigorous.
questions.explanation: Line coverage is weakest, branch coverage checks both sides of each decision, and path coverage checks combinations (rarely full).

questions.prompt: Match each item to its role in coverage practice.

pairs.right: Tools that collect and report coverage
The untested lines/branches to act on

questions.explanation: Use the tools and the Missing report to find gaps; don't turn the percentage into a target.
